newsitem.title: USA: Bush White House team revive old political battles.
newsitem.headline: Bush White House team revive old political battles.

text.p: Like old soldiers reliving their wartime experiences, former President George Bush and those who served in his administration rehashed old issues on Friday, including Bush's costly retreat on his 1988 "no new taxes" campaign promise.

The occasion was a Hofstra University conference on Bush's presidency that also included presentations by leading professors, political experts, diplomats and journalists. The conference opened on Thursday and will close on Saturday with a speech by former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev.

Bush, in a relaxed, freewheeling roundtable discussion with about two dozen Hofstra political science students, rejected "nit-picking ex post facto criticism" that as president he had been too timid in dealing with the collapse of communism in Europe and the fall of the Soviet Union.
"We did not want to stick a finger in Gorbachev's eye and cause the Soviet military to act in a way that we did not want ... democratic change came and it was free" of turmoil," he said.

Turning to other foreign policy matters, Bush said reunification of Germany was "a very interesting diplomatic problem" because it required overcoming the misgivings of Britain, France and Poland. And he said he still believes he was right to maintain U.S. relations with China after the 1989 military crackdown on dissidents.

"I'm absolutely convinced that there are more human rights and human liberties today that when Tiananmen Square occurred," Bush said, adding that he has been to China eight times as a former president. He was U.S. ambassador to China in the mid-1970s.

Bush, a Republican, was more philosophical than in the past about his defeat at the hands of Bill Clinton in 1992. "The people wanted change," he said. But showing his continued bitter dislike of the news media, which he feels treated him unfairly in the campaign, he said the press bears some responsibility for the "ugliness that exists in Washington."
Bush and his wife Barbara, who took part in a forum in the role of U.S. first ladies, were awarded honorary doctorates by Hofstra.

The academic proceeding also brought old scars to the surface from White House infighting over a 1990 budget accord with the then-Democratic Congress that led Bush to renege on "read my lips, no new taxes" -- the widely quoted campaign promise in his 1988 Republican convention speech.

Many former Bush aides privately agreed with Professor Richard Pious of Barnard University, who called Bush White House chief of staff John Sununu and Budget Director Richard Darman "clueless" in pushing the move.
"The tax card was played far too quickly" in negotiations with the Democrats, former Bush domestic policy adviser Roger Porter said.

Jim Cicconi, a former deputy to Sununu, said Bush's retreat on his tax pledge was "the most internally divisive issue" of his presidency, and had caused "very intense discussions and disagreements" among Bush's staff.

"I believe George Bush was convinced at the time that the economic health of the United States made a budget deal imperative in 1990," said Cicconi. He added that Bush's retreat on the tax pledge was a "political tragedy" that probably cost him re-election in 1992.
